newsitem.title: USA: California judge upholds Santa Clara's tax plan.
newsitem.headline: California judge upholds Santa Clara's tax plan.

text.p: A California judge dealt a blow on Thursday to the state's anti-tax movement, ruling that a controversial half-cent sales tax approved by 52 percent of Santa Clara County voters was valid.
The ruling, by Superior Court Judge Jeremy Fogel, could open the door for similar tax measures by other cash-strapped counties in the state, attorneys who sued Santa Clara warned.

Santa Clara County's Measure B -- a nine-year, half-cent sales tax that would raise $1.2 billion -- was approved by 52 percent of voters last November. The measure said the tax was to be used for "general county purposes."
An adjoining "advisory" measure -- Measure A -- listed highway and transit projects that would be funded by Measure B. The advisory measure was approved by 78 percent of voters.
Under California law, most general taxes require a simple majority to pass. Most special taxes, raising funds for specific programs or services, require two-thirds approval.

Santa Clara's twin tax measures attracted statewide attention, from other counties as well as anti-tax groups. Several other counties in the state said they may try to duplicate Santa Clara's approach.
In January, the Santa Clara County Taxpayers' Association filed suit along with other groups.

They charged that Measure B was unconstitutional because the county planned to use revenues from the tax to fund projects identified in Measure A. They argued Measure B was in reality a special tax requiring two-thirds voter approval.
But Fogel said there were no legal restrictions barring use of Measure B tax revenues to fund Measure A transportation projects.

"The fact that the two measures appeared together does not alter the undisputed fact that Measure A is explicitly advisory...and that Measure B explicitly contains no restrictions or limitations on the use of tax revenues," the judge said in his written ruling.
Attorney Bob Rychlik, who represented opponents of the tax, said the ruling set a "dangerous precedent."
"If the judge's ruling is allowed to stand, it would just pull the teeth out of tax limitations in this state," he said.
He said the association plans to appeal the decision.
